strengths: Novel plasticity framework: The definition of plasticity as expected rate of change provides an intuitive and principled way to characterize component adaptability, distinct from worst-case Lipschitz bounds
Rigorous theoretical analysis: Propositions 1-4 systematically derive upper bounds for LayerNorm, feedforward, and attention modules, with Prop 4 providing tighter bounds under energy constraints
Extremely thorough experimental validation: ~800 finetuning runs across 11 benchmarks with multiple seeds and learning rates, complemented by extensive gradient dynamics analysis (Figs 19-51)
Consistent empirical findings: Plasticity ranking (MHA → FC1 → FC2 → LN2 → LN1) holds across all benchmarks and scales (ViT-Base, ViT-Huge), with performance correlating well with plasticity
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-structured paper with effective visualizations, detailed implementation details, and honest discussion of theoretical limitations

Mechanistic understanding: Gradient norm analysis convincingly demonstrates that high-plasticity components maintain larger gradient norms, providing explanatory power for observed finetuning benefits
weaknesses: Loose theoretical bounds: The attention bound (Prop 3) exhibits cubic growth in sequence length; empirical plasticity values are orders of magnitude smaller than bounds (Fig. 6: 10^8 vs ~10), substantially undermining predictive validity

Indirect connection to finetuning: The link between input-output plasticity and finetuning performance relies on unverified assumptions about gradient flow (citing Béthune et al. 2024). The argument that ∇_x f amplitudes determine ∇_θ L is not rigorously established in this work

Artificial plasticity definition: P(f) computed over cross-domain token pairs (pretraining vs downstream) rather than within the downstream domain where finetuning actually occurs, limiting alignment with the target problem

Limited scope and generalizability: Results confined to vision transformers and selective finetuning; extension to language models, other PEFT methods (LoRA, adapters), or joint component optimization unexplored. Only classification tasks and relatively small-scale models tested

Modest practical improvements: On many benchmarks (CIFAR-10, Contrast, Snow), MHA outperforms LN1 by <1% (Table 6). Larger gains (~4-6%) appear only on hard datasets (Clipart, Sketch), questioning practical significance

Theoretical assumptions insufficiently justified: Prop 1 restricts to shared mean/std across tokens; the restriction to bounded token sequences in Prop 3 is informal; sensitivity to radius r unexplored

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 800+ finetuning runs across 11 benchmarks, two model sizes, and multiple seeds demonstrating consistency of findings
Clear presentation and effective visualizations (Figs. 1-4) that clearly communicate the main insights
Detailed theoretical framework deriving upper bounds (Propositions 1-4) for different transformer components, providing principled component ranking
Novel perspective framing finetuning adaptability through plasticity (average rate of change) rather than traditional smoothness metrics
Extensive appendix with full proofs, implementation details, and training dynamics across all datasets supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Loose theoretical bounds differing by orders of magnitude (10^6×) from empirical values, suggesting bounds capture worst-case rather than typical behavior; the gap undermines theoretical explanatory power

Indirect connection between theory and practice: link from Lipschitz bounds → gradient norms → better finetuning lacks rigor, especially since lower Lipschitz constants are preferred in other ML contexts

Limited novelty of core insight: plasticity is a standard average sensitivity measure; the main empirical finding (attention modules are better) confirms Touvron et al. (2022) without providing new, actionable insights

Narrow experimental scope limited to vision transformers and image classification; no exploration of other architectures, domains, or multi-component finetuning scenarios that reflect real-world practice
Marginal empirical improvements often within error bars (e.g., CIFAR10: MHA 98.91±0.07 vs LN1 98.67±0.03); minimal statistical significance testing (only one Wilcoxon test) weakens claims

Incomplete causal mechanism: paper shows correlation between high plasticity and finetuning success but doesn't establish causality; alternative explanations (architectural factors, intrinsic flexibility) not excluded
Artificial experimental setup: finetuning components in isolation doesn't reflect practical scenarios; no analysis of interactions when jointly finetuning high-plasticity modules
Missing key ablations: evolution of plasticity during training, sensitivity to pretraining objectives, and why LayerNorms have low plasticity by design are unexplored
Limited baseline comparisons: no comparison with other selective finetuning methods (BitFit, IA3, etc.) or alternative component selection strategies; full finetuning results show only marginal gaps

Restrictive theoretical assumptions: bounded token assumption validated on single appendix figure; image energy bound may not generalize; Proposition 1's assumption that tokens share mean/std at each position is questionable

strengths: Novel plasticity framework unifying component adaptability analysis
Rigorous theoretical analysis with formal upper bounds on all major ViT components
Comprehensive experiments: 11 benchmarks, ~800 finetuning runs, multiple seeds and model scales
Strong empirical validation of theoretical predictions with consistent ranking across tasks
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details and extensive ablations
Clear presentation with effective visualizations communicating key intuitions
Practical guidance with statistical significance testing
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: attention upper bounds ~10^8 vs empirical ~8 plasticity, raising questions about whether theory captures relevant phenomena
Theoretical assumptions are restrictive (identical token statistics, bounded image energy) and pretraining-specific, limiting generalizability
Component-wise finetuning analysis unrealistic; no evaluation of multi-component finetuning where findings might not hold
Limited scope: vision classification only; no validation on NLP or other tasks despite claiming relevance to LLMs
Findings largely confirmatory of prior work (Touvron 2022, Ye 2023, Zhao 2024); novelty is in explanation rather than discovery
Performance improvements modest: MHA vs FC1 = 0.07%, many results within standard deviation of competing methods
Plasticity definition appears somewhat ad-hoc; limited justification for why average rate of change is the 'right' measure vs alternatives
Mechanistic understanding incomplete: intuition about gradient norms is plausible but causality unproven and deeper analysis lacking
Missing analysis: plasticity evolution during finetuning, comparison with other PEFT methods, interaction effects between components

strengths: Rigorous theoretical framework with formal upper bounds on plasticity for different ViT components (Propositions 1-4)

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental validation: ~1000 finetuning runs, 11 benchmarks, multiple model sizes (86M-632M), both optimizers (SGD/Adam), multiple seeds, low-data regimes, and extension to other architectures (DINOv3, GPT2)
Clear, well-written presentation with effective visualizations (especially Fig. 1 and 3) that effectively communicate intuition and findings
Excellent reproducibility support: detailed implementation details in appendix, promised code release, transparent carbon footprint reporting (259 kgCO2eq), and full hyperparameter documentation
Practical actionable guidance for practitioners: identifies that attention modules and feedforward layers merit prioritization over LayerNorms during finetuning
Good empirical-theoretical alignment: Figure 3 demonstrates correspondence between theoretical plasticity rankings and empirical measurements across diverse benchmarks
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: plasticity upper bounds are several orders of magnitude looser than empirical measurements (Fig. 7 shows ~10^8 theoretical bound vs ~10 empirical), raising questions whether theory captures actual mechanisms

Tenuous causal connection between plasticity and finetuning performance: the claimed chain 'high plasticity → large gradient norms → better finetuning' is demonstrated empirically but lacks formal justification; why should larger gradient norms necessarily improve adaptation rather than causing instability?
Modest practical improvements: ~1% average gain (90.8% MHA vs 89.8% LN1 across benchmarks) is relatively small and may not justify adoption costs in practice

Limited novelty beyond prior work: Touvron et al. (2022) already showed empirically that adapting attention modules works well; this paper provides theoretical post-hoc explanation rather than enabling fundamentally new approaches

Vague definition of plasticity in practice: Definition 1 uses 'uniform distribution over distinct pairs of sequences' that is underspecified; procedural implementation mixes pretraining and downstream data but this crucial detail appears only in appendix

Strong but incompletely justified assumptions: (1) Proposition 1 assumes identical token statistics across images, justified by ImageNet normalization but not validated for downstream datasets with different distributions; (2) Proposition 3 requires bounded tokens (x ∈ B^n_r), a non-trivial assumption not empirically validated
No comparison to alternative component adaptability metrics (condition numbers, alternative Lipschitz estimators, gradient sensitivity measures)
Limited scope and absence of proposed methods: paper identifies which components to finetune but proposes no novel algorithms or adaptation strategies to exploit these insights

Incomplete analysis of important factors: Why doesn't full finetuning of all components achieve comparable results? When might high plasticity be undesirable (e.g., catastrophic forgetting)? How sensitive are results to downstream task properties?

strengths: Extensive empirical validation with ~1000 finetuning runs across 11 datasets, multiple model sizes, and two optimizers, demonstrating consistency of the plasticity ranking across diverse settings
Novel perspective: arguing that non-smooth (high plasticity) components benefit transfer learning, departing from conventional wisdom that smoothness aids generalization
Clear presentation with informative visualizations and comprehensive implementation details supporting reproducibility; code is promised
Consistent findings across different architectures (ViT, DINOv3, GPT2) and domains, with well-structured theoretical framework (Propositions 1-4)
Effective connection between plasticity and gradient magnitudes (Figure 5), providing intuitive support for the proposed mechanism
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior empirical work: Touvron et al. (2022), Ye et al. (2023), and Zhao et al. (2024) already showed empirically that attention and feedforward layers are better for finetuning; the paper claims theoretical justification but the connection is indirect and non-rigorous

Massive confounding by parameter count: MHA/FC layers have ~28M parameters vs. ~18K for LayerNorm (1500x difference), yet parameter count is not adequately controlled despite being a simpler explanation for the results

Theoretical bounds are extremely loose: Figure 7 shows attention plasticity upper bounds are 10^6-10^8 times larger than empirical values (~6-7), raising questions about whether these bounds are informative or predictive of which components to finetune

Weak causal justification: the argument linking plasticity to finetuning (high Lip(f) → large gradients → better optimization) is indirect, relies on citations for key steps, and doesn't rigorously establish why input-output smoothness should predict parameter adaptation quality

Plasticity definition not ablated or justified: why average rate of change rather than variance, max rate, or gradient-based metrics? No ablation studies validate this critical choice, nor is sensitivity to (x,y) pair sampling explored
Unrealistic experimental design: isolating components for finetuning is impractical—practitioners finetune combinations. Relevance of single-component results to real-world scenarios is unclear
No practical algorithmic contribution: the paper identifies which components to finetune but proposes no new methods that leverage these insights, limiting actionable value

Causality vs. correlation unresolved: plasticity could be a proxy for other factors (capacity, expressiveness, initialization), not causally important; paper demonstrates correlation but not causation

Modest improvements with weak statistical rigor: performance gains are often small (e.g., 90.8% vs. 89.8%); improvements are verified with 5%-level tests without quantifying effect sizes or practical significance

Limited theoretical novelty: Propositions 1-4 apply straightforward techniques (normalization factors, spectral norms, existing Lipschitz bounds from Castin et al. 2024); deriving tighter bounds or novel bounds would strengthen the contribution

strengths: Novel theoretical perspective on transformer adaptation through plasticity that challenges conventional wisdom about smoothness
Exceptional experimental scale with ~1000 finetuning runs providing high confidence in consistent findings across 11 benchmarks, multiple model sizes, and architectures (ViT, DINOv3, GPT-2)
Solid theoretical grounding with formal plasticity bounds for different components and clear connection to parameter gradient behavior
Findings remarkably consistent across diverse settings: multiple optimizers (SGD, Adam), pretraining paradigms (supervised, self-supervised), and datasets
Excellent presentation with clear intuition (particularly Figure 1), detailed proofs, and honest limitations discussion
Strong reproducibility with released code, comprehensive implementation details, and careful hyperparameter documentation
Practical insight showing single-component finetuning (especially attention) competitive with LoRA despite using 15× fewer parameters
weaknesses: Limited practical applicability: analyzes single-component isolation while practitioners typically finetune multiple components jointly or use methods like LoRA; component interactions unexplored
Modest absolute performance improvements (~1% in many cases) despite consistent relative gains; unclear if improvements justify architectural considerations
Loose theoretical bounds, especially for attention (O(√(3n + (12n+3)r⁴))); Definition 1's uniform distribution over token pairs may not reflect actual optimization dynamics

Causation not definitively established: plasticity-performance correlation is shown, but the proposed mechanism (plasticity → large gradients → faster learning) relies on intuition rather than rigorous proof
Limited analysis of when plasticity matters most: on easy datasets with high linear probing performance, plasticity differences are minimal but not thoroughly discussed

Architectural specificity: analysis tailored to transformer blocks; generality to non-transformer architectures and other domains unclear despite DINOv3/GPT-2 extensions still within transformer family
Single-component finetuning artificial simplification: real adaptation might show different plasticity preferences when multiple components interact; joint adaptation not explored
